Akin means similar in nature, quality, or character. When you say something is akin to something else, you are saying those two things share a deep, essential resemblance — not just a passing or coincidental likeness, but a resemblance in what they fundamentally are.

Think of it this way: two things that are "akin" are cut from the same cloth. They may not be identical, but they share something at their core — the same feel, the same essence, or the same kind of quality.
The One Grammar Rule You Must Know

"Akin" is always followed by the word "to." The structure is always:

[Something] is akin to [something else].

You would never place "akin" directly before a noun. You would not say "an akin feeling." Instead, you would say "a feeling akin to sadness" or "this feeling is akin to sadness." That distinction — placing it after a verb like is, was, feels, seems — is non-negotiable in standard English.
Examples That Show the Meaning Clearly

"His restlessness was akin to madness."
He wasn't actually mad, but his restlessness had the same wild, uncontrollable quality that madness has.

"Learning to code is akin to learning a new language."
The two activities share the same fundamental nature: both require you to learn a new system of rules, structure, and logic from scratch.

"The grief she felt at leaving that city was akin to losing a close friend."
The grief wasn't identical to losing a person, but in its depth and emotional weight, it resembled that experience closely.

This is the key nuance. "Similar" is a flat, neutral word. "Akin" carries more weight. When you use "akin to," you're making a stronger, more thoughtful claim — that the resemblance runs deep, not just on the surface.

Consider the difference:

"That feeling was similar to fear." — Fine, but plain. It merely notes a likeness.

"That feeling was akin to fear." — Stronger. It says the feeling shared the very nature of fear — the same quality at its core.

Because of this, "akin" is often the word a writer reaches for when they want to illuminate a connection that isn't immediately obvious but is genuinely meaningful. It signals: "Pay attention — these two things are more alike in their essence than you might think."
The Two Senses of the Word

The common, living sense is the one described above: meaningfully similar in nature or quality. This is the sense you will encounter and use almost every time.

The rare, old-fashioned sense is: related by blood or family. You might occasionally encounter this in older texts — for example, "The tribes were akin to one another." In modern English, this meaning is nearly obsolete. You can acknowledge it exists, but you will almost never need it in practice.

"Akin" sits in the slightly formal register. You will encounter it more often in writing — essays, journalism, literature, speeches — than in casual conversation. That said, it is not a rare or obscure word. It is perfectly natural and appropriate in everyday writing, and a thoughtful speaker might comfortably use it in conversation too.
The Complete Picture in One Sentence
"Akin to" means essentially similar in nature or quality — it draws a meaningful comparison between two things that share the same fundamental character, and it is always followed by "to."
